purpose: Practice ownership changes between Core 12 routes without adding unreviewed records to the published assessment case set.
boundary: These are synthetic authored study drills. They reuse source-supported route boundaries but are not published assessment cases and do not change factual-review or verification state.

drills.title: The price looks wrong after the sales-order context changed
drills.scenario: A synthetic sales order has a valid-looking condition record, but the final price differs from the expected commercial result after a document-context change.
drills.prompt: Decide whether the first wrong layer belongs to sales-order context or pricing. Build the shortest evidence path that proves the owner before changing a condition record.
expected_reasoning: State the expected commercial result and document context.
Confirm the relevant sales-order inputs and control level.
Confirm the pricing procedure before checking one condition record.
Trace condition eligibility, access, runtime key, record, and calculation only after the procedure is correct.
Stop at the first divergence and explain the blast radius of changing shared configuration.
Prove the corrected order price and any billing impact.
drills.boundary_question: Which upstream sales-order decision can change the pricing path even when the condition record itself is valid?
red_flags: Creates a new condition record before proving the procedure and runtime key.
Treats every pricing symptom as owned by Pricing configuration.

drills.title: Late confirmation: Shipping date or ATP promise?
drills.scenario: A synthetic sales order has physical stock, but the requested delivery date is not confirmed. A route change was introduced recently.
drills.prompt: Separate logistics-date construction from availability. Show how you would prove whether Shipping created the wrong requirement date or ATP correctly rejected the promise.
expected_reasoning: Reconstruct delivering plant, shipping point, route, calendars, and scheduling dates.
Identify the material availability date consumed by the availability check.
Reconstruct ATP relevance, quantity, scope, and supply-demand picture.
Inspect advanced allocation/protection controls only after the base requirement and date are correct.
Name the first owner where expected and actual paths diverge.
Prove both the confirmation and the executable downstream delivery path.
drills.boundary_question: Is ATP wrong, or is it correctly evaluating the wrong upstream date?
red_flags: Changes ATP scope before checking the material availability date.
Changes transit time only until the final date looks acceptable.

drills.title: Goods receipt exists, but procurement is not financially complete
drills.scenario: A synthetic purchase order has a goods receipt and usable stock, while Finance still shows an open GR/IR balance after the team believes the purchase is complete.
drills.prompt: Explain which completion layers are already proven and which are not. Diagnose without using a manual journal as the first fix.
expected_reasoning: Confirm the procurement requirement, PO, and receipt history.
Prove the inventory event and resulting stock state.
Check whether the matching invoice receipt exists and represents the same business quantity/value.
Treat physical receipt and invoice completion as separate events.
Explain whether the open GR/IR state is expected timing or a real mismatch.
Reconcile source documents and journal evidence before correction.
drills.boundary_question: Which module owns the missing business event, and which module only shows its financial consequence?
red_flags: Clears GR/IR manually without finding the missing or mismatched source event.
Calls the process complete because stock is available.

drills.title: Production confirmed, stock missing, cost still open
drills.scenario: A synthetic production order has operation confirmations, but the finished quantity is not in the expected stock and the order still carries unsettled cost.
drills.prompt: Explain why one green production status is insufficient. Build the completion proof across execution, stock receipt, and financial settlement.
expected_reasoning: Separate planned state from shop-floor execution evidence.
Confirm what quantity was actually confirmed and consumed.
Trace the expected goods-receipt event and material document.
Prove the resulting inventory state and any warehouse handoff.
Separate production-order execution from controlling settlement.
Close only when physical and financial completion reconcile.
drills.boundary_question: Which completion layer is open: execution, stock receipt, or financial settlement?
red_flags: Treats confirmation as proof of goods receipt.
Treats technical completion as proof of CO settlement.

drills.title: Quality accepted the material, but warehouse stock is still unusable
drills.scenario: A synthetic inspection lot has an acceptance decision, but the operational team still cannot use the stock in the warehouse.
drills.prompt: Separate the quality decision from stock disposition and warehouse execution. Find the first layer that did not consume the intended decision.
expected_reasoning: Confirm the inspection context and recorded quality decision.
Check whether the inspection lot is stock-relevant for the intended stock posting path.
Prove the expected Inventory Management stock state after the quality decision.
If EWM is involved, prove whether warehouse stock and execution state represent the same disposition.
Identify whether the defect is quality authority, inventory posting, or warehouse synchronization/execution.
Close with usable stock and reconciled evidence, not only an accepted usage decision.
drills.boundary_question: Did Quality make the wrong decision, or did Logistics fail to consume a correct one?
red_flags: Moves stock manually before proving the usage-decision consequence.
Blames QM because the warehouse stock is blocked.

drills.title: Master data is approved but the consuming process still fails
drills.scenario: A synthetic Material change request is approved and active in the governance system, but Sales and Procurement still use an old or incomplete organizational view.
drills.prompt: Separate governance completion, replication, mapping, and consumer-process usability. Decide who owns the first correction.
expected_reasoning: Confirm the governed business requirement and approved active record.
Check whether the required organizational attributes are inside the governed scope.
Trace replication, filtering, mapping, target receipt, and reconciliation.
Confirm which version the Sales and Procurement processes actually consume.
Avoid local repair until the authoritative/replication boundary is understood.
Prove business usability in at least one consuming process after correction.
drills.boundary_question: Does approval prove consumer usability, or only the governance decision?
red_flags: Repairs the target system locally without protecting the governed source of truth.
Treats workflow approval as proof that all consumers received the record.

drills.title: The integration monitor is green, but the business object is wrong
drills.scenario: A synthetic inbound sales message shows successful technical processing, but the receiver has a duplicate or incomplete business object.
drills.prompt: Prove message identity, receiver commit state, duplicate protection, and business reconciliation before replay or closure.
expected_reasoning: Identify the exact business message and expected idempotency key or identity contract.
Trace transport delivery separately from receiver application processing.
Determine whether the receiver committed the expected business object once, more than once, or not completely.
Check ordering and duplicate/retry semantics before any replay.
Use the sales-order state as business evidence, not middleware status alone.
Close only after technical and business states reconcile.
drills.boundary_question: Which green status is proven: transport, application processing, or business completion?
red_flags: Replays the message because the business result looks wrong.
Closes the incident because middleware is green.

drills.title: Delivery exists, but warehouse execution never starts
drills.scenario: A synthetic outbound delivery is due and visible upstream, but no expected warehouse task is available for picking.
drills.prompt: Separate the shipping/delivery state from EWM warehouse-request and task creation. Find the first missing execution object.
expected_reasoning: Confirm the upstream delivery and execution context are actually due and relevant for the warehouse.
Identify the EWM warehouse request representing the business demand.
Check whether a warehouse task should exist and which determination or release step creates it.
Separate task creation from warehouse-order grouping and queue assignment.
Do not alter shipping dates to repair a warehouse execution problem unless the demand itself is wrong.
Prove the final warehouse confirmation and upstream process update.
drills.boundary_question: Is the business demand missing, or is EWM failing to turn valid demand into warehouse work?
red_flags: Changes the delivery to force EWM without proving the warehouse request.
Treats missing warehouse task and wrong warehouse order as the same failure.
